Neonatal Smooth snakes (Coronella austriaca) emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs following a period of incubation that is heavily influenced by thermal conditions. Field observations indicate that hatchlings, upon eclosion, typically measure approximately 15 centimeters [Lb = approximately 15 centimeters] in snout-vent length, a modest size that reflects the substantial yolk reserves invested by the female prior to oviposition. This initial body length places the species well within the range documented for other small-bodied colubrids found across temperate Europe. The neonate's physical state at emergence is further characterised by its wet body mass. Newly emerged individuals consistently weigh around 3 grams [Wwb = around 3 grams], a surprisingly low mass given their snout-vent length and one that underscores the elongate, slender morphology typical of the genus Coronella. This combination of a relatively long body and a minimal mass likely facilitates the hatchling's immediate capacity for cryptic movement through leaf litter and dense groundcover, where it must locate its first prey item amidst a habitat teeming with potential predators. The fine balance between initial size and mass at this earliest life stage is therefore a critical determinant of early survival probabilities in the wild.

As individuals progress through their growing juvenile phase, they undergo a substantial increase in both length and mass before attaining reproductive maturity. Field studies conducted on central European populations have provided valuable data on the body size thresholds associated with the onset of breeding activity. Females typically reach their ultimate snout-vent length at approximately 55 centimeters [Li = approximately 55 centimeters], while males also achieve a comparable maximum body length, with the ultimate SVL for males also recorded at 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters]. This lack of pronounced sexual size dimorphism is a notable feature of the species' life history and contrasts with the pattern observed in many other Eurasian colubrids where females are substantially larger. Alongside this growth in linear dimensions, juveniles must accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of reproduction. Available data suggest that the threshold mass for sexual development corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of about 30 grams [Wwp = about 30 grams]. Attaining this critical mass appears to be a more reliable predictor of reproductive competence than body length alone, reflecting the need for adequate fat storage to fuel gestation and, in females, the production of a clutch of yolked eggs.

Under controlled laboratory conditions designed to mimic the thermal regime of their natural habitat, specifically at a constant temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the timing of key life history events has been quantified for this species. The age at which captive individuals first exhibit reproductive behaviour, marking the transition from the immature stage to the reproductively active adult phase, is estimated at roughly 1,643 days after hatching [tR = roughly 1,643 days after hatching] at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This protracted period to first breeding is characteristic of a slow-lived, K-selected life history strategy and is considerably longer than the maturation times reported for more rapidly developing colubrids. The data indicate that under these thermal conditions, individuals invest several years in somatic growth and fat accumulation before channeling resources into gametogenesis and the associated reproductive behaviours. This delayed maturation likely enhances lifetime fitness by ensuring that individuals are of sufficient size and condition to compete for mates and successfully incubate a clutch without compromising their own somatic integrity.

The reproductive output of adult female Smooth snakes, when examined under the same thermal conditions of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], reveals a pattern of low fecundity consistent with their slow life history. Data from both field and captive populations indicate that females do not breed annually, instead they produce a single litter every other year once they have achieved full adult size. The maximum reproductive rate achievable in this species can be understood by considering the components of this cycle. A gravid female gives birth to a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] only once every two years [F_R_i = once every two years], with litter sizes typically ranging between 2 and 8 live young. This biennial reproductive schedule is a direct consequence of the considerable energetic investment required to sustain a pregnancy in a temperate climate where active foraging periods are limited. The extended interval between successive reproductive events allows females to fully replenish their depleted energy reserves, a necessity that likely limits the population's intrinsic rate of increase and renders the species vulnerable to habitat fragmentation.

Long-term mark-recapture studies have provided robust estimates of the maximum lifespan potential for Coronella austriaca under semi-natural captive conditions. When maintained at a constant temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], representing the average summer conditions within their active season, the maximum recorded longevity is approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years]. This is one of the longer lifespans documented among European colubrids of similar body size and aligns with the species' general slow pace of life, characterised by late maturity and low annual reproductive output. This extended reproductive window, spanning potentially a decade or more, allows individuals to compensate for their infrequent breeding by producing multiple litters over their lifetime. An individual that commences reproduction at 4.5 years after hatching [tR = 4.5 years after hatching] under these thermal conditions could theoretically participate in several biennial breeding cycles before reaching senescence at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. The combination of a late age at first reproduction, low fecundity, and exceptional longevity is a classic demographic syndrome associated with stable, low-mortality environments such as the dry, rocky heathlands this species favours.
